hints: Look first at where the CH2OH group is attached in each ring. Glucose only has one CH2OH, on the carbon next to the ring oxygen.
For the true glucose structures, now focus on carbon 1 on the right side of the ring and check if its OH is on the same side as the CH2OH or the opposite side.
walkthrough:
**Sort glucose from fructose**

Both glucose and fructose with formula $C_6H_{12}O_6$ can form six-membered rings. The quick check is the $CH_2OH$ groups.

In glucose, only carbon 5 (top left, next to the ring O) carries $CH_2OH$. In fructose, the anomeric carbon (top right, next to the ring O) also carries $CH_2OH$.

**Recall the alpha rule for glucose**

In the ring form, carbon 1 is the anomeric carbon on the right. The rule is simple and visual.

For $\alpha$-glucose, the OH on C1 is trans to the $CH_2OH$, so it points down and away. For $\beta$-glucose, the OH on C1 is cis to the $CH_2OH$, so it points up on the same side.

**Apply to A, B and D and pick B**

Option C has $CH_2OH$ on the right side carbon, so it is a fructose ring, not glucose. Options A, B and D all have $CH_2OH$ only on the top left, so they are glucose types.

Only B shows the C1 OH pointing down, opposite to the $CH_2OH$ up. That is the classic $\alpha$-glucose arrangement.

options.A: This is glucose but the OH on C1 points up on the same side as the CH2OH. That cis arrangement is beta-glucose, not alpha-glucose.
options.B: This has CH2OH only on the top left carbon and the OH on C1 points down, trans to CH2OH. That is the defining arrangement of alpha-glucose.
options.C: This has CH2OH on the right-side anomeric carbon as well as on the left, which is characteristic of fructose, not glucose.
options.D: Although the C1 OH points down, the OH positions on the other carbons do not match glucose. It is a different hexose epimer, not alpha-glucose.
